pharm: Blocks both alpha-1 and non-selective beta adrenergic receptors, lowering blood pressure by reducing peripheral vascular resistance without major reflex tachycardia.
quick: 100 mg PO twice daily (titrate); IV bolus 20 mg for emergencies
Take with or just after food to improve absorption
Caution; reduce dose, risk of hepatotoxicity
May worsen postural hypotension; limit intake
BP, heart rate, postural symptoms, LFTs if indicated
summary: Labetalol is a combined alpha-1 and non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker used to treat hypertension, including severe hypertension and hypertensive emergencies (IV), and is a preferred agent in pregnancy-associated hypertension. It lowers blood pressure by reducing systemic vascular resistance while limiting reflex tachycardia. It is well tolerated but can cause postural hypotension, fatigue, and, rarely, hepatotoxicity.
indications: Hypertension (oral, alone or with other agents)
Controlled blood-pressure reduction in clonidine withdrawal or pheochromocytoma (specialist use)

dosage.d: Start 100 mg twice daily; titrate by 100 mg BID every 2-3 days. Usual 200-400 mg twice daily (max 2.4 g/day)
dosage.n: Take with food; titrate to BP and tolerance

dosage.d: 20 mg slow IV over 2 min; then 40-80 mg every 10 min as needed (max total 300 mg)
2 mg/min infusion titrated to response (usual effective dose 50-200 mg)
dosage.n: Stop infusion once target BP achieved

dosage.d: 100-200 mg twice daily, titrated; max about 2.4 g/day

admin: Take oral tablets consistently with or just after food
For IV use keep the patient supine during and shortly after dosing; do not let the patient stand for several hours
Use continuous or frequent BP and heart-rate monitoring during IV therapy
Do not stop oral therapy abruptly - taper to avoid rebound hypertension/angina
Stand up slowly to limit dizziness
moa: Labetalol competitively blocks both alpha-1 (postsynaptic) and beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors. The alpha-1 blockade causes vasodilation and reduces peripheral vascular resistance, while concurrent beta blockade prevents the reflex tachycardia that would otherwise accompany vasodilation. The net effect is a fall in blood pressure with relatively little change in cardiac output, making it useful for rapid yet controlled BP reduction.

absolute: Bronchial asthma / severe reactive airway disease
Second- or third-degree heart block (without pacemaker)
Severe bradycardia, cardiogenic shock, sick sinus syndrome
monitor: Hepatic function if symptoms suggest liver injury

preg: One of the preferred antihypertensives in pregnancy, including chronic hypertension and pre-eclampsia, based on extensive clinical use. Monitor the neonate for bradycardia, hypotension, and hypoglycaemia after delivery when used near term.
lact: Small amounts are excreted in breast milk; considered compatible with breastfeeding. Observe the breastfed infant for bradycardia and signs of beta-blockade.
renal: No dose adjustment required in renal impairment; labetalol is extensively metabolised by the liver and not significantly removed by dialysis.
hepatic: Use with caution and consider lower doses in hepatic impairment. Rare but serious hepatocellular injury (including fatal cases) has been reported; discontinue if liver injury is suspected and do not rechallenge.

major: Verapamil / diltiazem and other negative chronotropes (additive bradycardia and AV block)
Clonidine (risk of rebound hypertension if clonidine stopped; stop labetalol first)
interactions.food: Food increases oral bioavailability; take consistently with respect to meals.
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may potentiate postural hypotension and dizziness; limit intake.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause false-positive increases in urinary catecholamines/metanephrines (interferes with assays for pheochromocytoma).

emergency: Signs of hepatic injury (jaundice, dark urine)

monitoring: Blood pressure (sitting and standing) and heart rate
Symptoms of heart failure or bronchospasm
Liver function tests if hepatic symptoms occur
Fetal/neonatal heart rate when used in late pregnancy
counsel: Take with or just after food and at the same times each day
Do not stop suddenly - this can cause chest pain or a rise in blood pressure
Stand up slowly; report fainting, severe dizziness, or shortness of breath
Report yellowing of skin/eyes, dark urine, or unusual tiredness (possible liver effect)
Inform your doctor if you have asthma, diabetes, or heart problems
pk: Oral 20 min-2 h; IV within 2-5 minutes
Oral 1-2 h; IV effect peaks 5-15 min
Oral about 8-12 hours; IV effect lasts hours
Store at 20-25 C; protect from light; do not freeze injection
pearls: Combined alpha/beta blockade lowers BP without major reflex tachycardia - useful in hypertensive emergencies
Preferred oral and IV antihypertensive in pregnancy and pre-eclampsia
Keep patient supine during IV dosing; orthostatic hypotension is common after IV use
Watch for rare hepatotoxicity - investigate and stop if liver symptoms develop
missed: Take the missed oral dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and continue your usual schedule - do not take a double dose.
overdose: Overdose causes severe hypotension and bradycardia. Place the patient supine with legs raised. Treat bradycardia with atropine, bronchospasm with beta-agonists, and refractory hypotension/bradycardia with IV fluids, glucagon, and vasopressors; consider transvenous pacing. Labetalol is not effectively removed by dialysis.
